## Report: Does CoQ10 Improve Movement Symptoms in Parkinson's Disease?

**Conclusion: No.** The weight of high-quality evidence does not support CoQ10 as an effective treatment for improving movement (motor) symptoms in Parkinson's disease.

**Evidence trajectory:**

An earlier Phase II trial suggested promise—CoQ10 at doses of 300, 600, and 1200 mg/day was safe and well-tolerated, and hinted that it might slow progressive impairment as measured by the Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) ([NINDS](https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/clinical-trials/effects-coenzyme-q10-coq-parkinson-disease)). A related early report similarly noted CoQ10 "appears to slow the progressive deterioration of function in PD, but these results need to be confirmed in a larger study" ([JAMA Neurology](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/782965)).

However, the definitive test was a large, phase III, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial led by Beal and colleagues, specifically designed to confirm or refute the earlier findings. This rigorous trial found that CoQ10 treatment did **not** slow progression of PD and showed no clinical benefit ([JAMA Neurology / Johns Hopkins](https://pure.johnshopkins.edu/en/publications/a-randomized-clinical-trial-of-high-dosage-coenzyme-q10-in-early-/)). Coverage of this result was described as CoQ10 having "struck out" in its definitive Phase 3 test, reversing the optimism generated by the smaller preliminary study ([Alzforum](https://www.alzforum.org/news/research-news/coenzyme-q10-strikes-out-phase-3-parkinsons)).

**Why the answer is "no":** This case exemplifies why small early-phase trials can be misleading. The initial encouraging Phase II signal did not replicate in a properly powered, definitive Phase III RCT—the gold standard for testing whether a treatment truly works. When larger, better-controlled trials failed to confirm benefit, the scientific and clinical consensus shifted to conclude CoQ10 does not meaningfully improve PD motor symptoms or slow disease progression.

**Bottom line:** Despite biological plausibility (CoQ10's antioxidant/mitochondrial support role) and early hope, definitive Phase III RCT evidence contradicts any real motor benefit from CoQ10 in Parkinson's disease.
